title: Overhead Hoists
summary: Chain, lever and air hoists hold a load overhead, so the rated load, the support and where you stand all matter. This talk covers OSHA's overhead hoist requirements.
talking_points: The manufacturer must indicate the safe working load on the hoist, and it must never be exceeded (29 CFR 1926.554(a)(1)).
The structure holding the hoist must have a safe working load equal to that of the hoist (1926.554(a)(2)).
Supports must let the hoist move freely and must not keep it from lining up with the load (1926.554(a)(3)).
Install the hoist so the operator can stand clear of the load at all times (1926.554(a)(4)).
Air hoists need an air supply with enough capacity and pressure, and air hoses must be positively connected so they cannot come loose in use (1926.554(a)(5)).
Overhead hoists must meet the manufacturer's requirements for design, installation, testing, inspection, maintenance and operation (1926.554(a)(6)).
Unsafe equipment must be tagged or locked out, or removed from service, until it is fixed (1926.20(b)(3)).
Good practice: never stand or work under a suspended load, and check the hoist and its hook before each lift.
site_hazards_to_check: Hoist with the rated load missing or unreadable
Overhead support not rated for the hoist load
Hoist hung where the operator has to stand under or beside the load
Air hoist hose not securely connected
Hoist with a damaged chain, hook or controls still in use
No manufacturer inspection or maintenance record
discussion_questions: How do we confirm the rated load of this hoist and of what it hangs from?
Where should the operator stand when the load is lifted?
Who tags out a hoist that fails its inspection?
